title: An Old Result, Still Moving
paragraphs: In 1929 Edwin Hubble published evidence that galaxies beyond our own are, on average, moving away from us, and that the more distant a galaxy is, the faster it appears to recede. The relationship is roughly proportional: a galaxy twice as far away recedes about twice as fast. Hubble relied on measurements of redshift, many of them made earlier by Vesto Slipher, and combined them with his own estimates of distance.

The finding is often misread as a picture of galaxies flying outward from a central explosion. In the standard interpretation, based on general relativity, it is space itself that expands, so observers in any galaxy would see the same pattern of recession and none occupies a privileged centre. The light from distant galaxies arrives shifted towards the red end of the spectrum, and the shift grows with distance.

Credit for the discovery has also been revisited. The Belgian priest and physicist Georges Lemaitre had predicted a link between distance and recession speed and estimated the rate of expansion in a paper of 1927, two years before Hubble's. It appeared in French in a Belgian journal and attracted scant attention for years. In 2018 members of the International Astronomical Union voted to recommend calling the relation the Hubble-Lemaitre law.

The rate of expansion, known as the Hubble constant, remains surprisingly hard to pin down. Measurements based on nearby stars and supernovae give a noticeably higher value than those inferred from the cosmic microwave background, the faint afterglow of the early universe. Whether this gap reflects hidden errors or physics missing from current models is unresolved, which suggests that even a result nearly a century old can still yield surprises.

options.explanation: Yield burada üretmek, doğurmak anlamındadır: eski bir sonuç hâlâ sürpriz doğurabilir.

Trafikte yol vermek anlamı bu bağlama uymaz.
